transcript.speaker: Giselle Rousseau
transcript.content: Hey Zane Bennett — I’m heading out for a residency and I’m really torn about leaving my partner behind. You travel a lot; how did you cope when opportunities pulled you away from someone you cared about? I’m looking for practical ways to keep us connected and make the distance feel like part of a shared goal — routines, check-ins, projects together, anything that helped you.

transcript.speaker: Zane Bennett
transcript.content: Hey Giselle — I’ve done this a few times. What helped me was predictable touchpoints (a weekly video call and a quick good-morning voice note) and turning the distance into something collaborative: we made a shared playlist, traded daily photo prompts for a little zine, and scheduled overlapping “studio hours” so we felt like we were working toward the same thing. Be explicit about expectations, plan visits, and agree on what “success” looks like for both of you — when I skipped that clarity relationships strained, but when we treated the time apart as a shared project it actually brought us closer.

transcript.speaker: Giselle Rousseau
transcript.content: Thanks, Zane — that’s exactly the kind of roadmap I needed. I like the shared-project idea (photo prompts and overlapping studio hours feel doable) and the predictable touchpoints. My partner worries about feeling secondary — how did you phrase expectations and define “success” so it felt fair? Any tips for finding overlap during an intense residency schedule?

transcript.speaker: Zane Bennett
transcript.content: Phrase expectations around fairness and concrete actions — for example: “This residency matters to me and I want us to stay close. Could we try weekly video calls, a monthly visit, a shared project, and reassess in six weeks?” Ask your partner what would make them feel prioritized and set one non‑negotiable (a weekly date or a mid‑residency visit) so it isn’t just your schedule dictating things. Use shared tools (calendar, playlist, photo prompts), schedule overlapping studio hours for quiet companionship, and agree on a simple definition of success (both feeling connected and clear plans to reunite), then check back and adjust as needed.

transcript.speaker: Giselle Rousseau
transcript.content: Thanks, Zane — that actually helps calm the spiral. I’m thinking of proposing something like: “This residency matters to me, but you matter more — could we try weekly video calls, a monthly visit, and a small shared photo project (two prompts a week), then reassess in six weeks?” Does that sound fair and non‑threatening? Any wording or tweaks to make it feel less like a checklist and more intimate when my days get really packed?

transcript.speaker: Zane Bennett
transcript.content: That sounds really fair and thoughtful — I’d soften the checklist language and lead with care. Try: “This residency matters to me, and you matter more — would you be open to trying weekly video calls, a monthly visit, and a small shared photo project (two prompts a week) for six weeks, then checking in and adjusting?” Add one intimate, non‑negotiable (e.g. a short Sunday evening call or a daily ‘thinking of you’ voice note) and invite them to suggest changes so it feels collaborative, not prescribed.

transcript.speaker: Giselle Rousseau
transcript.content: Thanks, Zane — that wording feels warm and collaborative. I’ll try: “This residency matters to me, and you matter more — would you be open to weekly video calls, a monthly visit, and a small shared photo project (two prompts a week) for six weeks, then checking in and adjusting? Also could we keep a short Sunday evening call as our non‑negotiable?” One quick thing — when you were busiest, what tiny habit (5–10 seconds) did you use to make your partner feel seen?

transcript.speaker: Zane Bennett
transcript.content: I had a tiny ritual: a 5–8 second voice note each morning — sometimes a quiet ‘good morning,’ sometimes a little guitar riff or a quick line about something I’d seen that reminded me of them. It’s short, personal, and hard to shrug off; pick something that feels like you (a photo, a voice note, or one sincere sentence) so it stays intimate even on busy days.
